source.title: Perplexity Can Miss SAE Feature Damage Under Quantization

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures whether fixed SAE features remain aligned after model weight compression, refining the claim that SAE features are stable units by showing that their measured fidelity varies with quantization level, model, and read-out layer.
record.gate_note: The paper measures feature survival using a frozen SAE on identical tokens before and after compression. Perplexity results are not rows because they do not measure the claim versions' feature or representation properties. The logistic-regression AUC results predict feature survival but do not themselves establish whether SAE features are complete or canonical units.
record.test_reason: The study uses a frozen public SAE as a fixed measurement basis to audit how a model's activations drift under weight quantization and pruning. Its correlation-survival score measures whether a compressed model still matches the FP16 model in that basis. That is a related but different construct from V5. Feature drift in a perturbed model is expected and says nothing about whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units of the original model. V5's stability concerns the dictionary itself, such as cross-seed or cross-run variation, which the paper explicitly sets aside (Sec 2.1). No version is tested, so the results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that perplexity parity is insufficient evidence that FP16 SAE-based interpretability transfers to quantized models, and that feature survival is graded. They also stress two further findings the paraphrase omits. Survival is predictable from FP16 feature statistics, with peak activation the strongest marginal predictor. Quantization and matched pruning damage largely the same features. They call for feature-level audits and leave causal validation to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures frozen-SAE activation-pattern correlations before and after RTN quantization and matched magnitude pruning in language models; it does not reproduce the toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature survival varies with quantization bit width, model, and read-out layer. The paper also reports sensitivity to survival threshold; token-budget and sampled-subset checks show comparatively small variation.

fits_no_version.finding: Under RTN weight quantization, the share of FP16-active frozen-SAE features with correlation >0.9 falls gradually. Pythia-70M layer 4: 98.3% (INT8) to 62.4% (INT6) to 14.5% (INT4). Gemma-2-2B layer 12: 99.1% to 51.3% to 12.4%. The drop is far smaller at Pythia layer 2 (94.7% at INT5). Perplexity can stay flat or improve while features degrade (Gemma INT7). Survival is predictable from FP16 peak activation (AUC 0.92–0.97). Pruning damages overlapping feature sets (Jaccard 0.79–0.86).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features fitted on a full-precision LLM remain aligned with a weight-compressed version of that model in proportion to compression severity, with weak-signal features drifting first.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to two model families, publicly available residual-stream SAEs, simulated RTN quantization, and specified token budgets and read-out sites. The paper measures correlation-based feature fidelity and perplexity, not causal consequences for steering or safety interventions; it explicitly leaves causal validation for future work. The Gemma pruning comparison is approximately rather than closely matched.
record.rows_left_out: Perplexity and pruning-calibration values are omitted because they do not themselves measure SAE feature stability. The paper's logistic-regression survival-prediction results are omitted because they predict survival rather than measuring whether features remain stable or canonical.

untested.parts: No toy models, no sparsity transition, no superposition geometry.
No test of capacity competition as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemantic neurons.
Uses pretrained SAEs but does not test whether features are distributed across neurons or recoverable by a dictionary.
Completeness, canonicality and cross-run stability of SAE features are not tested. Only drift of the compressed model's activations in a fixed SAE basis is measured.
No test of one-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 link conflates robustness of a frozen SAE readout under model perturbation with SAE features being canonical or stable units of the model. The paper itself treats SAE stability (seed variability) as a separate, complementary question. Reclassified as T4 (SAE used as an audit instrument). Row r13 has a wrong value.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test toy networks, sparse feature competition, superposition geometry, or a sparsity-dependent transition.
The paper does not test whether neurons are polysemantic because features compete for limited capacity, or whether importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
The paper does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
The paper uses SAE features but does not test whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or whether a dictionary can recover the model's features.

It tests activation-pattern stability of a frozen SAE basis under RTN quantization and matched magnitude pruning, not feature completeness, canonicality, stability across SAE training runs, or stability under other compression methods.
The paper does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.
